clue.text: A day to get around the Continent

parts.note: the article is taken at face value, one letter off the page
FRI is the diary abbreviation for Friday, so any 'day' may be three letters
CA is short for circa, the Latin for about or around, used before a rough date

explanation.walkthrough: The capital C on Continent points squarely at Europe, which is the one continent this cannot be. Circa is worth banking: 'around' or 'about' is very often just those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Africa is one of the seven continents; the capital C teases the British habit of meaning mainland Europe by 'the Continent'.

clue.text: Multiple sentences with no escaping e.g. penguins?

parts.note: flight is what you take when you flee — a prisoner in flight is escaping
the suffix that means 'with no' is a word in its own right here
bird is old prison slang for a stretch inside, so sentences are birds

explanation.walkthrough: The slang comes from birdlime rhyming with time, which is why a stretch inside is bird. Everything in the surface — sentences, escaping — belongs to a jail, and none of it belongs to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Penguins are birds whose wings drive them through water instead of air, so they stand as one example of the whole class.

clue.text: Some progress when visiting Greek island, reportedly

parts.note: a guest who is visiting is in, the way a host at home is in

indicators.note: Something reported is passed on by ear, so what matters is the sound of the word and not its spelling.

parts.note: the Greek island is Rhodes, and said aloud it is spelt the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The setter never says which island, because only the sound of it counts — a homophone of a place name is Everyman's stock in trade, and it works on the ear alone.
explanation.definitionFit: You make inroads into a task — advances driven into ground that was resisting you, which is what progress amounts to.

clue.text: Concession for entrance

definitions.meaning: conceding a point in an argument is admitting it
the way in, and the price on the sign beside it

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on the verb admit — admitting a fact, admitting a visitor. The surface reads as a ticket office offering cheap entry, which is a third sense the clue never uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A concession is something you admit; entrance is being admitted. Both senses come straight off 'admit', one mental and one physical.

clue.text: Slovenly type's got some neck!

definitions.meaning: the unshaven, unpressed sort who looks like he dressed in the dark
not the whole neck but the loose skin at the back of it

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'some neck!' as cheek — the nerve of the man. The setter means the anatomy, the bit you would pick up a kitten by.
explanation.definitionFit: A scruff is an unkempt, badly turned-out person, and the scruff is also the loose skin at the nape that a cat is carried by.

clue.text: Rope material is brought into stable regularly

indicators.note: Bringing something into a word puts it inside, so the letters part company and let it sit between them.
Doing a thing regularly means at a steady interval, so take every other letter and keep the rhythm.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of STABLE, keeping the steady beat
the little verb is taken as two letters and dropped inside

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tidy picture of a stable yard, which is exactly what makes 'regularly' read as a habit rather than as an instruction about letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is the stiff fibre stripped from agave leaves and twisted into rope, twine and matting.

clue.text: Songwriter's payment: Taylor collected Japanese currency

indicators.note: Things collected are gathered up in whatever order they come to hand, so the letters need not stay as they were.

parts.note: the surname goes into the mixture whole, all six letters of it
Y is the symbol for the yen, and single-letter currencies are a setter's staple

explanation.walkthrough: The surname is left deliberately bare, so you cannot tell which Taylor is meant and start hunting for a first name. Seven letters is a short mix — write them out before guessing.
explanation.definitionFit: A royalty is the cut a writer earns every time the song is played or sold: payment by usage rather than a flat fee.

clue.text: 'Term'; 'oath'; 'news'; 'chat'?

parts.note: the surface offers a list of unrelated nouns and dares you to say what they share; count the items, then count the letters in each
the item that gives the game away, because a sworn oath and a shouted curse are the same word, and the phrase being defined usually means the second

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here: the clue is four demonstrations of itself, and the semicolons are only there to make it look like a quiz question.
explanation.definitionFit: Each quoted item is spelt with exactly that many characters, and 'oath' carries the swearing sense the phrase is normally reaching for.

clue.text: Everyman has potential to improve, solver: honestly

parts.note: the setter writing about himself is I or ME — here he signs his own name
a player who shows promise has it in him to get better
the person on the other side of the clue is you

explanation.walkthrough: Setter and solver written into the same clue is Everyman's signature move, and both conventions are worth banking: the byline is I, and whoever is reading is YOU.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Honestly' is the interjection thrown in to insist you mean it, which is the whole job of this three-word phrase.

clue.text: Caught by fabled avian, one with dozens of teeth

parts.note: C for caught comes off a cricket scorecard, where it stands before the fielder's name
the roc is the giant bird of the Sinbad voyages, large enough to carry off an elephant

explanation.walkthrough: Two crossword regulars in four letters. The surface has the bird doing the catching, which is why nothing warns you that 'Caught' is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A croc is a crocodile, and a crocodile carries some sixty teeth at a time, replacing them throughout its life.

clue.text: Cake decorator's instructions returned with two cuts

indicators.note: To return is to come back the way you went, so what is left is read from its far end.

parts.note: the instructions for making a cake are its recipe
two letters are lopped off the end, the P and the E, leaving four

explanation.walkthrough: Cakes, decorating and instructions all belong to one kitchen, so nothing in the surface hints that one of those words is there only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The icer is the one who spreads the icing, so the job title comes straight off the sugar coating they apply.

clue.text: Eyre hears a line that needs cutting in preparation for performance

indicators.note: A cutting is a strip snipped out of a longer text, so the answer is trimmed free of the words on either side of it.

parts.note: the answer runs on from the tail of the name, through the next two words, and stops at the first letter of the last

explanation.walkthrough: Eyre, a line, a cut: those three words make a theatre out of the clue, and the theatre is there to stop you reading the letters as one continuous string.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is the run-through a company works at before an audience is let in: practice held for the sake of the show.

clue.text: Small athletic club in purple

parts.note: lil is little with the middle worn away, the spelling of a nickname
AC is the athletic club on a hundred sports badges, from AC Milan down

explanation.walkthrough: AC is the half most solvers see first; the informal 'lil' is the harder half, and it is the sort of spelling a setter can only use in short answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac names both the shrub and the pale purple of its blossom, so it is a particular shade rather than the full colour.

clue.text: Company constructed silos: they're enormous

definitions.note: 'They're enormous' describes the answer instead of replacing it: it tells you to expect a plural of huge things, not an adjective you could swap in.

indicators.note: Anything constructed has been put together out of parts, and parts put together afresh rarely go back in the order they arrived.

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation on any company's letterhead
the five letters of the grain towers, rebuilt in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze giant standing over a harbour, and the Latin plural is what 'they're' is quietly telling you to expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Colossi are giant statues — the Colossus of Rhodes and its kin — so sheer size is the whole of what the word carries.

clue.text: Conman's retiring, wanting rest badly

indicators.note: Rest taken badly is broken rest, and letters broken up come back in a different arrangement.

parts.note: a retiring person is shy, hanging back rather than leaving a job
the four letters of rest, shaken into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a crook giving up the trade and craving a holiday, so 'retiring' looks like leaving work. The word the setter wants is the timid sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A shyster is a disreputable operator, usually a crooked lawyer, who works the small print rather than picking pockets.

clue.text: Wavy at the edges, building collapsed

indicators.note: Read it as the verb: to build is to assemble something from pieces, and these pieces go up in a different order.

parts.note: nine letters taken whole, straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: A building that collapsed is a picture you accept without a second look, and that is what stops you noticing that one of those two words is material and the other is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Scalloped means edged with a row of shallow curves, like the rim of a scallop shell — the pattern, not the seafood.

clue.text: A little garland is dainty, getting scorn

indicators.note: A little of something is a part of it, not the whole, so only a stretch of these words is wanted.

parts.note: the answer starts inside the first word and finishes inside the last, running straight across the middle one

explanation.walkthrough: Garlands, daintiness and scorn make a sentence that means something, and a sentence that means something is the best cover a setter ever has.
explanation.definitionFit: Disdain is scorn with a cold shoulder in it: contempt for something you consider beneath your notice.

clue.text: Ascertain age of potential partner

definitions.meaning: what a laboratory does to a bone or a pot, carbon and all
the person you have arranged to meet, and hope to meet again

explanation.walkthrough: Carbon dating and a Friday night are the same four letters in different worlds, one a verb and one a noun, which is the whole of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: To date a fossil is to work out how old it is; a date is also the person the evening has been arranged with.

clue.text: A card game? Cut

parts.note: the article stands as its own letter at the front
bridge is the card game crosswords lean on hardest, usually for its bidding

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting that plenty of other games would have fitted the words — it is the length and the letters that pick this one.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a book is to cut it down to a shorter version while keeping the sense: the editor's kind of cutting.

clue.text: Bin meat that's rotten all around

indicators.note: Meat gone rotten has broken down, and material that has broken down is free to re-form as something else.

parts.note: seven letters from two short words, mixed together

explanation.walkthrough: Bin and meat sit together so naturally that neither looks like fodder, and 'rotten' looks like a comment on the meat rather than an instruction about its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient describes whatever surrounds you — ambient noise, ambient temperature — the conditions on every side rather than any one source.

clue.text: Give evidence of risk: Barbie's boyfriend accepting love

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in, so the letters on either side open up and let it sit between them.

parts.note: a bet is money put at risk on an outcome
love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, and nothing is written as O
Ken has been the doll's boyfriend since 1961

explanation.walkthrough: Two conventions in one short clue: love for nothing comes off a tennis scoreboard, and the nothing is written as a letter O rather than a zero.
explanation.definitionFit: To betoken is to be a token or sign of something — dark clouds betoken rain — which is evidence short of proof.

clue.text: Right-winger offering two extremes in tyranny?

indicators.note: A word's extremes are its first and last letters, and here they close around what has gone before.

parts.note: the two ends of the word, its opening letter and its closing one
'or' is the little word that offers a choice between two things

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting the surface is unkind: a right-winger dealing in tyranny is a joke, not a definition, and only the letters are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tory is a British Conservative, so the label names a place on the political spectrum rather than a temperament.

clue.text: Send back — drive back, perhaps, potato?

indicators.note: Sending a thing back turns it to face the way it came, so its letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: to rebut a charge is to drive it back, and 'perhaps' admits it is one of several words for that

explanation.walkthrough: Two backs in a row, and only the first is an instruction. The question mark does the work of 'for example', since a potato is one of many.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato is the best-known tuber: a swollen underground stem that stores the plant's food, so the example points at the class.

clue.text: Lofty structure from which it's announced: 'It's time for girdles'

indicators.note: What is announced is taken in by ear, so the words are written down as they sound rather than as they are spelt.

parts.note: a girdle is a belt, the band that goes round the waist
the hour is the time being called, the way a bar calls happy hour
say those two words in one breath and they run together into the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the announcement itself: the tall thing that tells a town what time it is, telling it that it is time for belts.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell tower is built high so its peal carries — campanile, steeple, belfry — which is why height is the point of the thing.

clue.text: Author Dan is toast

definitions.meaning: the novelist who wrote The Da Vinci Code, named by his first name only
what a grill does to bread, taken as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Is toast' is slang for doomed, which is what the surface wants you to hear about the novelist, and it hides a plain surname beside a plain cooking verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Dan Brown wrote The Da Vinci Code; and to brown bread under a grill is to toast it — a surname and a cooking verb.

clue.text: Re-do the pork: awkward bloomer

indicators.note: An awkward thing sits wrong however you put it down, so these letters will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: eleven letters from three words, the hyphen counting for nothing

explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is a blunder as well as a plant, and the surface is so busy being a kitchen disaster that the garden never occurs to you.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a plant that flowers, and this garden perennial sends up flame-coloured spikes every summer.

clue.text: One authoritarian at back of boat

parts.note: one of a thing is a thing, so 'one' is the article A
an authoritarian parent is humorless and severe, quick to lay down the law

explanation.walkthrough: The strict sort and the back of a vessel are the same five letters, and the clue quietly uses one to build the other without ever pointing at the coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is the sailor's word for behind a vessel or towards its stern, which is the rear end of the hull.

clue.text: One primarily dominant, yet nepotistically appointed, securing throne?

definitions.text: One primarily dominant, yet nepotistically appointed, securing throne?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so nothing counts in each word but the letter it opens with.

parts.words: dominant, yet nepotistically appointed, securing throne
parts.note: the opening letter of each of those six words, taken in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the whole sentence as the definition as well: the description of the man and the instruction for spelling him are the same words.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynast rules by family line, so a portrait of someone dominant and installed by relatives reads straight as well as cryptically.
